catalog_quote: Betonung. Was die Betonung betrifft, so kann man es als stehende Regel betrachten, dass beinahe alle Wörter in ihrer nackten Form, d. h. wenn sie nicht in Verbindung mit anderen Wörtern gebraucht werden, den Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe haben. In der Rede erleidet der Accent jedoch mancherlei Verschiebungen, z. B.: kú-dsa kommen. ni-ma-kúdsa ich bin gekommen. ni-ku-dsá-ni ich bin am kommen. ka-dsá-ri? wann kam er? kámba er sagte. kambádsi? was oder wie hat er gesagt?
sweep_summary: Single works with stress in the title, Philippson 1991 (542-pp Paris V thesis on tone and accent in East Bantu), was located as an open full text on the DDL Lyon site (http://www.ddl.cnrs.fr/Fulltext/philippson/these.pdf; theses.fr says 'accessible: non', SUDOC lists only the thesis and an ANRT microfiche), downloaded to, and read at every Pokomo mention (27 hits, 18 pages). It refines and effectively contradicts the catalog's 'fixed-unreviewed penult' coding from Würtz 1889: Pokomo is an accentual (n+1 scheme) language in which a single lexical H falls on the penult, the final, or the first stem syllable and some words have none (pp. 41-42, 81, 415-416, 469), the penult carries a length but not a pitch culmination (p. 483), and after a historical penult attraction the language developed a strict word accent unaffected by the phrase (pp. 495-496). Recommended reclassify: lexical pitch accent / restricted tone with penultimate length culmination, deciding source Philippson 1991 pp. 81, 483, 495-496 (supersedes Würtz 1889), with the caveat that Philippson's Pokomo data rest on Whiteley's 6-pp vocabulary list and his own notes and he calls the language poorly known. A thesis summary (Philippson 1998, Faits de langues 11-12) exists on Persée but its PDF is altcha-protected (low priority). Bibliographic records (theses.fr, SUDOC, IdRef, DDL page) saved alongside; HAL, archive.

new_statements.quote: pokomo (groupe XVIII) : mahumbo, "entrailles"; mákwaɸa, "aisselles"; maʃóká, "haches". [...] Toutes ces langues peuvent, certes, s'analyser comme étant accentuelles, en ce que seule une syllabe est mise en valeur sur le plan prosodique (il n'y a que trois schèmes à chaque fois), mais la mise en rapport des schèmes réalisés et des syllabes accentuées sous-jacentes est évidemment problématique et réclame une analyse serrée, que nous entreprendrons au cours des chapitres qui suivent.
new_statements.translation: pokomo (group XVIII): mahumbo 'entrails'; mákwaɸa 'armpits'; maʃóká 'axes'. [...] All these languages can, certainly, be analysed as accentual, in that only one syllable is prosodically prominent (there are only three schemes each time), but relating the surface schemes to the underlying accented syllables is obviously problematic and demands a close analysis, which we shall undertake in the chapters that follow.
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse d'État, Université Paris V. p. 81 (Chapitre trois, commentary on Tableau II, the '(a) : 3' languages); see also pp. 41-42, 415-416, 469, 483, 495-496.
new_statements.reading: Pokomo is coded by Philippson as an accentual language with n+1 lexical schemes: one syllable per word may carry a lexical H (accent), some words carry none (mahumbo), and the accented syllable is not fixed -- first stem syllable (mákwaɸa), penult (ɲóka, mukóno, ŋkúku, mpémbe) or final (ɲumbá, ʃoká) -- with H-spreading to the penult being post-lexical. The penult has only a length culmination, not a pitch one (p. 483), and word accent is strict, unaffected by the phrase (pp. 495-496). This is not a fixed-penultimate stress system; the penultimate prominence Würtz 1889 heard is the demarcative penult lengthening plus the frequent penult H. The catalog's 'fixed penult' coding should become 'lexical pitch accent / restricted tone with penultimate length culmination' (consistent with the Nurse 2008 App. 2 present-vs-future accent contrast already held by the project). Caveats: Philippson's own Pokomo data are thin (Whiteley's 6-page list plus own notes) and he himself calls the language 'assez mal connu et par conséquent douteux' (p. 42); Upper vs Lower Pokomo is not distinguished.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Agree with the substance; three refinements. (1) In mákwaɸa the H sits on the class-6 prefix ma- (antepenult of the word), not on the "first stem syllable"; the three nominal patterns on p. 81 are therefore: no H (mahumbo), H on the prefix/antepenult (mákwaɸa), H on penult+final (maʃóká = BH ʃoká of p. 415 with the post-lexical leftward doubling). (2) What Philippson calls post-lexical is the leftward doubling of the H ("la double association à gauche du H est un phénomène post-lexical", p. 495; kuóna ɲumbá surfacing as kúóna ɲúmbá, p. 494; cf. "anticipation tonale", p. 187). The rightward "a…

audit.recode_to: Keep penultimate as the default word accent, but expect to add a restricted/grammatical tone-or-accent qualifier (verb TAM distinguished by accent placement, e.g. Lower Pokomo present hu-na-gúy-a vs future hú-na-guy-á) once Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 (Philippson addendum) is read; 'the exceptions statement: none-stated' and the the primary-stress rule's claim that all shifts are 'the penult rule re-applying' should not survive
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: confirmed verbatim on the page image we hold (Würtz 1889 p. 163 'Betonung') and in the full-volume scanned; it is the article's only accent statement. (2) Deciding source: an 1889 29-pp missionary grammar sketch, impressionistic, hedged ('beinahe alle Wörter'; accent 'erleidet.. mancherlei Verschiebungen' in speech). Held modern items are silent (Ipu 1982 excludes stress/tone; Shume 2017 syllable structure only; Meinhof 1905 only notes possible 'Tonhöhen' pairs). Glottolog and the record itself point to two unheld authoritative treatments (Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993, 780 pp, with Philippson's tone addendum; Philippson 1991/92, 542 pp). (3) A copies we hold already refines the classification: Nurse 2008 App. 2 p. 27 gives Lower Pokomo hu-na-gúy-a 'we buy' vs hú-na-guy-á 'we will buy' -- accent placement, not segments, distinguishes present from future, so accent is not invariably penultimate
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. opened (Würtz 1889, ZAS II p.163, 'Betonung'): the deciding quotation is there verbatim with all six examples (kú-dsa, ni-ma-kúdsa, ni-ku-dsá-ni, ka-dsá-ri?, kámba, kambádsi?), all penult. In the full-volume scanned, article = lines 38237-43440) a full-text search for stress/accent Beton|Accent|Ton auf|Tonh finds only this passage (article lines 365-370); no second accent statement. WÜRTZ'S OWN PARADIGMS (new page-level observation): rendered ZAS II p.179 (PDF p.186) at 300 dpi. Sporadic accent marks in the ka- and dsa-(future)

sources.quote: il est certain que le pokomo a subi le premier cycle d'assimilation; il suffit, pour s'en convaincre de prendre connaissance du schème des bases verbales longues : kuháɸíka < kuhaɸíka : "vomir" [...] Si l'attraction à la pénultième n'avait pas eu lieu, on attendrait le schème : *kúháɸika < *kuháɸika. Mais, par la suite, non seulement le pokomo n'a pas participé au deuxième cycle d'assimilation, il a même transformé son système en accent de mot strict, sans aucune influence du groupe prosodique, se distinguant ainsi de la plupart des parlers voisins. (pp. 495-496)
sources.locator: Pokomo (groupe XVIII, Sabaki) at pp. 41-42, 72, 78-79, 81, 187, 298, 415-416, 422, 469, 476, 483, 494-496, 515, 525; key passages p. 81, p. 483 (3.5.2 typologie), pp. 495-496 (Chapitre six, diachronie)
sources.note: Philippson treats Pokomo as an ACCENTUAL (restricted-tone / pitch accent) language, not a fixed: penultimate syllable stress language: (1) p. 41-42: Pokomo is the only 'pure' attested case of a language where some words carry no accent at all and no word carries more than one, 'assez mal connu et par conséquent douteux'; (2) p. 81: nominals show three schemes -- mahumbo 'entrailles' (no H), mákwaɸa 'aisselles' (H on the first stem syllable), maʃóká 'haches' (H on penult+final) -- 'seule une syllabe est mise en valeur sur le plan prosodique'; (3) pp. 415-416: reflexes of Common Bantu BB/HB/BH/…
